analysis: Brokskat ẓokur hair does not continue vāla. Compare the regional jakka/jaako hair or fleece family only provisionally: the final ur and sibilant/affricate onset require independent derivational and source evidence. Initial stress is observable without deciding that etymology.

Ushojo sʌṭʌk hammer is distinct from vardhira axe and the hand-hammer compound. A regional saṭak striking/tool formation is plausible, but no old input or accent can be established from the meaning alone; final stress remains recorded.
Ushojo danu axe handle could be a rod/shaft derivative, but neither vaṁśa nor ṭaṅka matches sufficiently. Its initial stress and final u are preserved while the ancestor remains unresolved.

Brokskat ɨɨs harvest is a verbal citation, not a grain/festival noun. Its final s may be the recurring verbal citation ending. A cutting/reaping root must be identified independently; neither granthana nor cīna is accepted by gloss overlap.
Brokskat pho he is unlike inherited sa/ana and resembles the Tibetan masculine pho element, but grammaticalization/contact must be demonstrated. No direct Sanskrit accent comparison is assigned.

SchmidtKaul2008pp247–248 explicitly identifies byaa mo hen, honey gliiitsi, kidney kxalma (with question mark), brok lightning, thakšaa loom and hin left as Purik loans. Database giaá'tsi and bin differ from those printed/source-discussion spellings and require reading corrections. Their accent belongs to loan adaptation, not inherited Shinaic sound change.

Brokskat alo tsib highest summer pasture is a multiword local terrain expression. The alo member could relate to high/up, but no identity with upakāla summer follows from the English gloss. Retain both components and do not assign an old accent.

Brokskat caris, naglis and zuy hill/mountain are distinct lexical alternatives and do not segmentally continue the khaṇḍa/skandha or dhārā sets. Regional terrain vocabulary and contact are plausible; each form remains separately attested rather than three accentual exceptions to mountain.
Ushojo ḍʌḍ honeycomb is a separate hive/material noun, not automatically a derivative of mākṣika honey. Reduplication or a regional container term may explain its shape; no old input is established.

Brokskat thanyaa thaa hungry is a predicative phrase. A nominal thirst/hunger base and copular element must be identified before comparing with udanyú; the long final-stressed first word cannot alone justify that reconstruction.

Ushojo kʌmʌn husband has final stress and differs from manuṣya, gharavāl and bhāriyāpa. A regional husband term or compound is possible; the final man portion alone is inadequate for selecting mánuṣa.

Ushojo kimi insect is a strong candidate for kŕ̥mi worm through loss of r and vocalic r to i, rather than kīṭa (which lacks m). The family is absent from the current linked Shinaic set; verify the full Turner entry and regional comparanda before accepting a new research family. Initial stress potentially preserves the old root accent.

Ushojo guṣi inside may be a locative related to house/goṣ rather than śriṣṭa; g must be explained independently. Retain as a spatial formation with initial stress and do not select the ancestor by final ši alone.
Ushojo laṛmun internal organs looks morphologically complex; a flesh/intestine compound is possible but not demonstrated. It is not assigned to liver or lung merely because of semantic adjacency.
Brokskat iṣka irrigation channel is not segmentally yavyā. A local canal or watercourse term, perhaps contact-derived, remains separate from giab; the exact source stress is unmarked.

Ushojo kiṣema is explicitly a present verbal form with final ma morphology and medial stress. A crushing/pounding root is plausible, but mardati is segmentally unsuitable; inspect the full paradigm before selecting an old root.
Ushojo caaku knife is the widespread regional cāku tool word, not a regular karttāra reflex. Its initial stress can inform loan adaptation but offers no secure inherited Vedic accent baseline.

Brokskat ẓaš may contain a contracted jñā/know base plus recurring s citation morphology, while Ushojo swɛma is a present form whose root is not identified. Neither is assigned to dakṣatvana or bhāvayati by semantic match alone; jñā requires comparative confirmation.

Ushojo stored down! bʌjala bo includes the tail of English lay down! in the form. The actual imperative phrase bʌjala bo requires a positional/adverb plus verbal analysis; it cannot be counted as a single old participle or root.

Ushojo abʌno left has initial a and medial b/n; the tempting comparison with kharva-derived khabo lacks the expected initial velar and must not be accepted from meaning. A prefixed or alternate left-hand term remains open.

Ushojo joŋ / pɑ̃ leg contains two alternatives. The pɑ̃ branch clearly belongs to pā́da after d loss; joŋ requires an independent limb-word etymology. Split the branches before any accent or family counts.

Ushojo nʌs lentil is not a regular mudga reflex. Compare a reduced masūra only provisionally because the initial n/m and missing ur need independent support; otherwise retain a regional pulse-name replacement.

Brokskat šus lie down probably contains the sleep root su/so plus citation s and could belong to svap/sup rather than a length noun. The š correspondence and paradigm are unverified, so keep it a candidate rather than a strict inherited link.

Ushojo asman palakin lightning contains the Persian sky word āsmān and a flash verb/noun. The phrase is not a direct simple vidyut reflex; the second member may be regional palak/flash but its etymology remains open.

Brokskat lyti lip does not straightforwardly match oṣṭha or tuṇḍa; source y may be a vowel. A local body-part replacement or heavy remodeling is possible, but no secure inherited input or accent is assigned.
